_meta.purpose: Ingredients worth knowing (D-132): what a primary source says about an ingredient that is not an additive, such as maida, palm oil or hydrogenated fat. Information only: nothing here changes a score, a band or a headline (D-004).
rules: Every sentence comes from a primary source read first-hand, with title, url, page and read_on (D-046). If no source says it, the row doesn't say it.

Say what the ingredient is, where it sits in the list and what the source says. Never unhealthy, healthy, safe, harmful, toxic, dangerous or free from; never about the brand (D-042, D-071). tests/test_ingredient_notes.py runs the wording lint on every sentence.
FSSAI decides what is permitted; ICMR-NIN and WHO are guidance and are quoted as guidance (D-086 keeps EU and US out entirely).
A row is shown only once Sushil has reviewed it (reviewed_by), as with data/additive_research.json (D-125).
Printed page = PDF page minus 17 for the ICMR-NIN guidelines; FSSAI compendium pages are PDF pages.

row_shape.title: the ingredient in plain words
names: whole words matched in an ingredient entry, lower case
ins: INS numbers that count as this ingredient (read by core/tokenize.py)
exclude: an entry containing one of these words is not this ingredient
row_shape.kind: refined_flour | milled_wheat | fat | oil_unnamed | fat_unnamed | sugar | sweetener | salt | caffeine
summary: one to three plain sentences
row_shape.position_rule: tile_if_top3 | tile | details | unnamed (the entry is only this name) | sugar_details (added to the sugar answer)
row_shape.children_only: true: shown only when a child's profile is on the phone
row_shape.reviewed_by: who reviewed it; null until then, and the row is not shown

not_rows.khandsari_bura_misri: Row 11 of the review is a change to normalization.json sugar_aliases, not a row here (FSSAI FPS&FA 2011 2.8.1 and 2.8.2, compendium XXVI PDF pp. 341 to 342).
not_rows.coconut_sugar: No FSSAI standard defines coconut sugar (searched compendium XXVI, 2026-09-29), so it is not added to sugar_aliases.
not_rows.nutrition_table: Row 15 of the review is phase 2 (D-133).

_meta.reviewed: All rows approved by Sushil 2026-09-29 ("approved, keep the oil line").

rows.title: Maida (refined wheat flour)
summary: Maida is refined wheat flour: wheat milled with the bran and germ essentially removed, as FSSAI's standard defines it.

ICMR-NIN says foods with sugar or refined carbohydrates have a high glycaemic index, so their glucose is absorbed quickly, and its guide to labels asks you to choose foods low in refined carbohydrates.
It groups maida with polished rice and polished millets (its Group B foods).

sources.title: FSS (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations 2011, 2.4.2 Maida, compendium version XXVI (20.12.2022)
ICMR-NIN, Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024

rows.title: Refined flour or starch
summary: ICMR-NIN counts refined flours of cereals, millets and legumes among its most processed foods (Group C), made by extensive processing of grains.
Its guide to labels names white flour and starch as refined cereals, and it says foods with refined carbohydrates have a high glycaemic index, so their glucose is absorbed quickly.
FSSAI's additive rules write corn flour as maize starch.

sources.title: ICMR-NIN, Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024
FSS (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations 2011, Appendix A, 6.2.1 Corn flour (Maize starch), compendium version XXVI (20.12.2022)

rows.title: Sooji (semolina, rava)
summary: Sooji (semolina, rava) is wheat ground or milled with the bran and germ wholly or partly removed, as FSSAI's standard defines it.

sources.title: FSS (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations 2011, 2.4.3 Semolina (Suji or Rawa), compendium version XXVI (20.12.2022)

rows.title: Palm oil
summary: ICMR-NIN names palm oil, with ghee, butter, coconut oil and vanaspati, as a source of saturated fat. It says saturated fat raises total and LDL cholesterol and the risk of heart attack and stroke.
WHO advises that no more than 10% of daily energy come from saturated fat, for everyone aged 2 and over, and lists palm oil among its sources.
Palmolein is the liquid fraction of palm oil, as FSSAI's standard defines it.

sources.title: ICMR-NIN, Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024
WHO, WHO updates guidelines on fats and carbohydrates (17 July 2023)
FSS (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations 2011, 2.2.1 (20) Palmolein, compendium version XXVI (20.12.2022)

rows.title: Hydrogenated fat
summary: ICMR-NIN says trans fats should be avoided. It describes hydrogenated fat, often called vegetable shortening, as vegetable oil partly hydrogenated so that some of its fat turns into saturated fat and trans fatty acids, which it says can increase the risk of heart disease and stroke.
Its guide to labels says foods that list partially hydrogenated oils "should not be acceptable". WHO advises that no more than 1% of daily energy come from trans fat.
FSSAI allows up to 2% trans fat by weight in vanaspati and bakery shortening.

sources.title: ICMR-NIN, Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024
WHO, WHO updates guidelines on fats and carbohydrates (17 July 2023)
FSS (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations 2011, 2.2.6 Hydrogenated vegetable oils, compendium version XXVI (20.12.2022)

rows.title: Coconut oil
summary: ICMR-NIN names coconut oil, with ghee, butter, palm oil and vanaspati, as a source of saturated fat. It says saturated fat raises total and LDL cholesterol and the risk of heart attack and stroke.
WHO advises that no more than 10% of daily energy come from saturated fat, for everyone aged 2 and over, and lists coconut oil among its sources.

sources.title: ICMR-NIN, Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024
WHO, WHO updates guidelines on fats and carbohydrates (17 July 2023)

rows.title: Ghee or butter
summary: ICMR-NIN lists ghee and butter as fats high in saturated fat and advises limiting them: 1 to 2 teaspoons a day, or none if possible.

sources.title: ICMR-NIN, Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024

rows.title: Margarine or fat spread
summary: Margarine is an emulsion of oils and fats with water, as FSSAI's standards define it. FSSAI allows up to 2% trans fat by weight in table margarine and in vegetable and mixed fat spreads.
FSSAI asks packs of food made with fats or oils to show the trans fat and saturated fat on the label.

sources.title: FSS (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations 2011, 2.2.5 Margarine and fat spreads, compendium version XXVI (20.12.2022)
FSS (Labelling and Display) Regulations 2020, 5(3)(c), compendium version I (23.09.2021)

rows.title: Vegetable oil, not named
summary: The oil isn't named on the pack.
FSSAI's labelling rules ask for the name of the specific edible oil in the ingredient list, such as mustard oil or groundnut oil.

sources.title: FSS (Labelling and Display) Regulations 2020, 5(2)(d), compendium version I (23.09.2021)

rows.title: Vegetable fat, type not named
summary: The type of fat isn't named on the pack.
FSSAI's labelling rules ask for the type of vegetable fat in the ingredient list, such as interesterified, fractionated or hydrogenated fat, or margarine.

sources.title: FSS (Labelling and Display) Regulations 2020, 5(2)(d), compendium version I (23.09.2021)

rows.title: Added sugar
summary: ICMR-NIN counts more than 25 g of sugar a day as high, and lists sucrose (table sugar), jaggery, honey, glucose, fructose and dextrose as added sugars.
WHO recommends that adults and children keep free sugars below 10% of daily energy, and says below 5%, about 25 g a day, would bring further benefits.

sources.title: ICMR-NIN, Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024
WHO, WHO calls on countries to reduce sugars intake among adults and children (4 March 2015)

rows.title: Sweeteners and children
summary: ICMR-NIN says children should avoid sugar substitutes, which it describes as sweetening agents such as aspartame, saccharin and sugar alcohols.
FSSAI counts sugar alcohols such as sorbitol, maltitol and xylitol as sweeteners.

sources.title: ICMR-NIN, Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024
FSS (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations 2011, 3.2.2 Sweetener, compendium version XXVI (20.12.2022)

rows.title: Salt
summary: ICMR-NIN counts more than 5 g of salt a day (over 2 g of sodium) as high, and names chips, sauces, biscuits and bakery products among foods high in salt.
WHO recommends that adults have less than 5 g of salt a day, under 2000 mg of sodium.

sources.title: ICMR-NIN, Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024
WHO, Salt reduction (fact sheet)

rows.title: Caffeine
summary: ICMR-NIN says tea and coffee contain caffeine, which stimulates the central nervous system, and advises moderation so that caffeine stays within 300 mg a day.

sources.title: ICMR-NIN, Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024
